full_article:
The NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite recorded the mountain moving weeks before the August 26 flood that killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal, but no one read the signal in time, according to a study by scientists at ISRO's National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad.

The paper, by 12 researchers and published in the Journal of Indian Society of Remote Sensing, is the first scientific account of the disaster in Rasuwa district, NDTV reported.

What The Satellite Saw

NISAR's L-band radar data from June 20 to August 19 showed an unstable, fast-moving zone exactly where the slope later failed, the study said.

Between July 26 and August 19, the displacement grew larger and more coherent, with some pixels shifting more than five metres horizontally.

The researchers said the warning became obvious only when compared with post-disaster imagery. NISAR, which cost $1.3 billion and launched on July 30, 2025, sends data down about every 12 days.

How The Disaster Unfolded

Around 99 million cubic metres of glacier ice and permafrost rock broke off a hanging glacier north of Langtang Lirung peak, at about 5,130 metres, on the morning of August 26. The study compared the volume to about 115 Empire State Buildings.

The debris fell roughly 2,170 metres in total and travelled about 5.9 km along the valley floor before turning into a flood. It hit a 72-km stretch of the Lhende Khola and Trishuli river systems, destroying roads, bridges, buildings and tunnels, including along the Nepal-China trade corridor.

A second landslide about three hours later created a debris-dammed lake.

Nepal's disaster authority put the toll at 1,451 dead and 5,745 missing as of September 21, according to figures cited in the study. The seismic signal recorded at 8:22 a.m.IST was the avalanche's impact, not its trigger, the paper said.

Climate Link And Limits

The researchers said satellite data showed an exceptionally warm summer in 2026, which would have increased melt and weakened already stressed slopes.

They warned that such cascading hazards may become more common, pointing to the 2021 Chamoli disaster in Uttarakhand.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory told NDTV that NISAR data is freely available through the Alaska Satellite Facility and ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal.

The study said satellites can show which slopes are unstable but cannot predict when one will collapse. That, it said, needs ground monitoring stations, along with automated, near-real-time analysis of the Himalayas' more than 25,000 glaciers.

title: Nepali community in Eugene comes together following deadly floods - Lookout Eugene-Springfield
description: Nepali community in Eugene comes together following deadly floods  Lookout Eugene-Springfield
publisher.title: Lookout Eugene-Springfield
full_article:
QuickTake: Eugene has maintained a sister-city relationship with Kathmandu, Nepal, since 1975. After flooding and landslides recently struck the country, the nonprofit supporting the connection gathered in grief and remembered how somewhere distant can feel close to home.

In late August, deadly landslides hit Nepal’s mountainous country, along the southwestern border of China. This historic event resulted in catastrophic destruction, with more than 1,400 people killed and ongoing searches for an estimated 5,000 others.

About a month later, additional fatal flooding in the same regions slowed relief efforts.

On the evening of Sept. 20, the Eugene-Kathmandu Sister City Association held a candlelight vigil for victims of the August disaster.

The association is the nonprofit supporting the tie between Eugene and the capital of Nepal, established in 1975 by Eugene mayor Les Anderson to promote peace, culture sharing and tourism between the two cities.

Eugene Mayor Knudson speaks at a vigil following the devastating flooding in Nepal as people set flowers and candles. Credit: Courtesy of Ken Beeson

Preeti Yonjon Feist, who moved to the United States from Nepal in 2006, sits on the organization’s board.

“It was really important we sat in our collective grief,” Feist, a hospice bereavement coordinator, said. “It was such a big thing, it felt sort of fake from here in the States, so it was imperative to remind folks it’s real.”

Fifty years since its start, the Eugene-Kathmandu Sister City Association is gaining attention with support from Mayor Kaarin Knudson. Celebrating the anniversary, she traveled to Nepal in March and spoke at the vigil before opening the floor to Feist.

“Grief isn’t personal; many times it occurs on an immense scale that stops us in our heels,” Feist said. “Grief has no boundaries. This complexity so many of us carry alone, so let’s hold space.”

Ken Beeson joined the organization about 10 years ago. He and his wife, Beth Eldridge, run their own nonprofit organization, the Kumari Project, which aims to empower and educate youth in Nepal through a safe house for at-risk children. The Kumari Project, which is not affiliated with Eugene-Kathmandu Sister City Association, is co-run by their Nepali daughter, Arun Storrs.

“We didn’t try to market the vigil as a big event. We didn’t want to distract from the reason we were there,” said Beeson, who is president of the Eugene-Kathmandu Sister City Association. “There was a solid turnout and anyone is always welcome, but we characterize many of our events for those with connection to Nepal.”

The association gets an annual $5,000 grant from the city of Eugene, which takes care of most expenses, except for a scholarship he helped create to support international Nepali students at the University of Oregon.

Mary Lou Vignola donated $50,000 to create the five-year scholarship in memory of her husband Frank Vignola. Started in 2024, it serves as “a testament to Frank’s lifelong commitment to education and his deep affection for Nepal.”

“The scholarship in Frank’s memory is fulfilling something he intended to establish,” said Vignola. “With Ken Beeson’s immeasurable help, it’s in place and helping to change a few lives.”

At the beginning of October, Beeson and Feist held an info table at DesiFest in Eugene to encourage interested people to get involved. Together, they share a goal of connecting with as many people as possible and expanding the board.

“If there are more people out there who might want to be part of our network, I’d love to talk with them,” Beeson said. “Our basic mission is to build friendship and connections between the citizens of Eugene and citizens of the capital of Nepal, Kathmandu.”

description: Anti-India Sentiment Era Is Over: Nepal's Finance Minister  Rediff

full_article:
Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle has said the era of linking nationalism in Nepal with anti-India sentiment is over, The Kathmandu Post newspaper reported.

‘The relationship between India and Nepal runs very deep. There are occasional problems, but we remain firmly connected. Nepal does not have a relationship with any other country like the one it has with India,’ Wagle told NDTV’s Padmaja Joshi at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi on Friday.

‘There was a time when nationalism in Nepal was associated with anti-India sentiment. But that era is over,’ Wagle said, The Kathmandu Post reported.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Wagle revealed, could visit India by the end of 2026, saying such a visit could help take Nepal-India relations to a new level, The Kathmandu Post reported.

After the August 26 disaster, Wagle, said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had called Balendra Shah and promised Indian assistance in full measure.

‘ In formal talks and official communications, India has consistently shown itself ready to help. It has made clear that it is prepared to provide whatever Nepal needs,’ Wagle said, The Kathmandu Post reported.

title: Not the best climate for climate finance - Nepali Times
description: Not the best climate for climate finance  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Nepal’s negotiators hailed the $21.6 million grant from the UN’s Loss & Damage Fund for the Trisuli Valley disaster on 26 August, but it was approved reluctantly, represents only 0.4% of the cost of recovery and reconstruction, and there are strings attached.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) this week provisionally approved the grant to Nepal for relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction two months after the flood catastrophe. It was announced in the run-up to a global climate summit (COP31) in Türkiye that starts 9 November.

Although Nepal is the first beneficiary of this scheme set up by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) during a previous climate summit in Egypt’s Sharm El-Sheikh in 2022, it came after three full decades of lobbying by developing countries for climate justice.

Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Waglé and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary wrote to the fund five days after the flood in August, seeking urgent assistance for a disaster they said was triggered by climate breakdown. Prime Minister Balendra Shah then made an impassioned speech at the UN General Assembly last month, calling for climate justice and solidarity.

Nepali officials have hailed the $20 million grant as a result of effective diplomacy and intense lobbying with the international community. However, some members of the FRLD Board at its extraordinary meeting on 22 October reportedly expressed reservations about the grant to Nepal, saying it should not set a precedent for pending claims by other countries to the Fund.

MILESTONE OR MILLSTONE?

“This landmark decision reflects the spirit of multilateral cooperation, climate justice and collective responsibility towards countries vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change,” said Maheshwar Dhakal of Nepal’s Ministry of Forests and Environment, who is currently serving with the FRLD from the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group.

“It is not only a significant milestone for Nepal but also a powerful message of hope and solidarity for developing countries,” he added.

Although Nepal has tried to put a brave face on the grant, $1.6 million of the $21.6 million will go for administrative costs, and the FRLD will have to approve a detailed proposal for where Nepal wants to spend the money. Rehabilitation and reconstruction will cost $4.7 billion, so the grant is only 0.4% of what is needed to rebuild.

Nepal’s Manjeet Dhakal is lead adviser to the LDC Chair on climate change, and says we should not expect the international community to accept all of Nepal’s demands, but added: “The fund was established for a purpose like this. And for the first time it has made a decision for our country, it’s symbolic and has long-term relevance in terms of setting a precedent.”

Only 1,500 remains of victims of the flood have been recovered, but at least 5,000 people are still unaccounted for. More than 60,000 people were directly affected by the flood, 15,000 of them children. Twelve operating and under construction hydropower plants generating 1,000MW were damaged or destroyed.

Climate skeptics have argued that the cascading disaster on 26 August was a result of geo-tectonic factors, and the heavy death toll and damage was because of recent settlements and infrastructure building along a vulnerable river valley, and cannot be entirely blamed on global warming.

In an interview with Nepali Times, Manjeet Dhakal disputed this: “We have enough resources and information such as World Weather Attribution strongly linking the floods to climate change and global warming.”

He says the Nepal government now needs to use its own rapid assessment of the damage, package them and submit a plan on utilising the fund for effective rehabilitation and reconstruction.

The Loss & Damage Fund operates through mechanisms like the Green Climate Fund (GCF) which in Nepal it works with accredited agencies like the Alternate Energy Promotion Centres (AEPC), the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) and NIMB bank for disbursement.

But experts say that ultimately it should be the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) that should lead the process because there may be bigger and more frequent Himalayan floods in future as the atmosphere warms.

“The $20 million was a limited fund for the short term, but our future preparedness needs serious consideration because there will be more and bigger disasters,” warns watershed scientist Madhukar Upadhyay. “Our strategy shouldn’t be to ask for money every time there is a disaster, it will never be sufficient and the funds are shrinking. We need to strengthen the capacity of local communities to deal with future disasters.”

The Nepal disaster will be front and centre of discussions at COP31 in Türkiye, and it will be an opportunity for its delegation to push the agenda of the vulnerability of mountain countries.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) released its Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return timed for the summit, warning that average global temperature would rise to 2.6°C above pre-industrial levels during this century. It said greenhouse emissions needed to be reduced by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2025 and 69% by 2040 to limit warming to 1.5°C.

“We are unlikely to hold the 1.5°C limit because the proposal to reduce fossil fuel dependence has been unpopular at recent COPs,” says Upadhaya, alluding to the United States and other countries backtracking on emission targets.

A 2.6°C rise would be catastrophic for the Himalaya which scientists say will then lose two-thirds of its remaining ice-cap, as glaciers shrink and the snowline moves up the mountain. If that happens, the Trisuli Valley flood will have been just a rehearsal for even bigger disasters to come.

High Asia is called the ‘Third Pole’ because it has the third largest volume of fresh water stored as ice, after the Arctic and Antarctica. If these ice caps melt, models show increased flow on Himalayan rivers until 2060 and steadily declining water volume thereafter for the 2 billion people who live downstream in Asia.

Says Manjeet Dhakal: “Despite economic downturns and geopolitics, the grant for Nepal shows that the international community is still committed to climate action. But it will not be enough to meet the consequences of a 2.6°C rise in global temperatures this century.”

title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet - DW.com
description: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet  DW.com
publisher.title: DW.com
full_article:
Dozens of people were confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday.

Nepali police said that authorities have recovered 157 bodies. Officers were "working to move families in flood-risk areas... to safer locations," police said.

"The pain and loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you that you are not alone in this difficult time — the state is with you with all its means and resources," Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a statement.

"Please be patient. The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together."

In China, authorities said at least three have died, with 265 still missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV ‌said.

Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At the same time, Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Security cameras captured the moment a wall of mud hit the Nepal-China border Image: REUTERS

Hundreds of people missing

Nepal's Tourism Ministry said 403 travelers were reported missing for several hours after the floods struck.

Missing travelers included 341 foreign tourists, among them were:

142 people from India

47 from the United States

34 from Australia

33 from Britain

24 from Canada,

At least 62 missing Nepali citizens

Other nationalities of those missing included people from

Malaysia

The Netherlands

Portugal

South Africa

South Korea

China's state news agency Xinhua reported Thursday that the number of missing people had increased to 558. State broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the missing people were foreigners.

The burst river also inundated villages in Dhading district Image: REUTERS

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday that 34 Australians were missing following the flash flooding.

"Our thoughts are with all those who will be concerned about their loved ones today," Albanese said.

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were also missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data."

What caused the flash floods?

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said an earthquake triggered an avalanche in the Himalayas that then triggered flash floods in the valleys below.

Xinhua said a mudslide on the Nepali side of the mountains spread to Gyirong County in Tibet.

"Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out," said David Fisher, the Nepal head of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepal's prime minister said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," Shah said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Rescue helocopters were initually unable to land due to the high floodwaters Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible," according to Chinese state media.

A second flood may be imminent, according to Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," he told the AFP news agency.

title: Former President urges global community to seriously take climate justice - The Rising Nepal
description: Former President urges global community to seriously take climate justice  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 24: Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari said the unprecedented natural disasters Nepal has experienced this year have once again underscored the gravity of this challenge, prompting a call to the global community to take Nepal's demand for climate justice seriously.

Addressing the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) conference organized by the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs, today, she outlined the state of climate justice that Nepal needs to achieve, according to her secretariat.

Bhandari cited examples linking global governance with climate justice while noting the Himalayas are a shared natural heritage closely connected to regional water cycles, biodiversity and ecological balance.

'In order to protect this vital ecosystem and mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change, it is essential to strengthen cooperation among Himalayan countries, including China, Nepal and India, in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers, developing early warning systems and coordinating disaster response,' she argued.

She also emphasized ensuring regional and international cooperation to strengthen to reduce climate risks, while ensuring sustained and reliable support from the United Nations and international financial institutions.

'Nepal advocates a world order in which relations among nations are guided not by power, but by international law, in which the voices of all nations are respected; and in which the concerns of weaker and vulnerable countries receive due consideration.' she asserted.

The former President emphasized the need to strengthen the United Nations as an effective institution that reflects the diversity and aspirations of the contemporary world to that end.

Peace and development are mutually reinforcing, she said, adding that ending poverty and hunger, promoting human well-being and redirecting resources spent on the arms race towards development are shared responsibilities of the international community.

'In accordance with the principle of leaving no one behind, we must make cooperation more effective in advancing inclusive, resilient and environmentally sustainable development.' Bhandari added.

She expressed her confidence that this forum will foster meaningful deliberations towards making the global governance system more just, inclusive and effective, while creating new opportunities for cooperation in pursuit of world peace, sustainable development and shared prosperity.

Highlighting that Nepal–China relations have evolved since ancient times through cultural exchanges, Buddhist philosophy and close people-to-people ties, Bhandari elucidated that our relationship rests on mutual respect, trust and cooperation. Also on the occasion, she expressed Nepal’s unequivocal commitment to the One-China Policy.

Respect for sovereign equality and for one another’s independence and territorial integrity is fundamental to sustaining enduring friendship and trust among nations, she stressed, calling for dialogue, cooperation and collective commitment to address the global challenges.

'The international order founded on the Charter of the United Nations, international law and multilateralism has made significant contributions to international peace, security and development. Nevertheless, reforms are necessary to make this system more inclusive, representative, transparent and effective in keeping with the changing global context,' the former President noted.(RSS)

By Mahendra Subedi, Xiong'an (China), Oct 24: Former President Bidya Devi Bhandari has called for stronger cooperation among Himalayan countries including Nepal, China and India in sharing meteorological data, monitoring glaciers, developing early warning systems and coordinating disaster response.

Addressing the 2026 Global Governance Forum in China’s Xiong’an city of Hebei Province earlier today, the former President said that global governance is also linked to climate justice and added that the unprecedented natural disasters Nepal experienced in August have underscored the gravity of the challenge. She noted that the Himalayas are a shared natural heritage connected to regional water cycles, biodiversity and ecological balance.

Likewise, she advocated strengthening the United Nations as an effective institution reflecting the diversity and aspirations of the contemporary world, adding that peace and development are mutually reinforcing. Ending poverty and hunger, promoting human well-being and redirecting resources from the arms race towards development are shared responsibilities, the former President added.

Delivering her speech in Nepali language, the former President expressed confidence that the Forum would foster meaningful deliberations towards making the global governance system more just, inclusive and effective, while creating new opportunities for cooperation for world peace, sustainable development and shared prosperity.

On Nepal-China relations, she noted that the bilateral ties have evolved since ancient times through cultural exchanges, Buddhist philosophy and close people-to-people links. She said the relationship is rooted in the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and rests on mutual respect, trust and cooperation, reaffirming Nepal's unequivocal commitment to the One-China Policy.

Likewise, Bhandari said the world is undergoing rapid scientific and technological transformation while facing serious challenges including economic inequality, poverty, geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, climate change and food insecurity. She was of the view that protectionism and unilateral approaches have complicated international cooperation, adding that such shared challenges cannot be resolved by any single nation and require dialogue and collective commitment.

The former president said that the international order founded on the UN Charter, international law and multilateralism has contributed significantly to peace and development, but reforms are needed to make it more inclusive, representative, transparent and effective.

"Global governance should not be shaped solely by the priorities of a limited number of nations," she said. "Differences among nations should be resolved through dialogue and diplomatic means," she added.

She further said the success of global governance should be measured by the positive changes it brings to people's lives.

The Forum was inaugurated by Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi on Friday evening.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s message was also delivered to the 2026 Global Governance Forum. “The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing,” Xi stated.

The Global Governance Initiative (GGI) was forwarded to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world, read the Chinese President’s message.

On the occasion, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang said all countries should uphold the multilateral trading system with the WTO at its core, keep development at the center of the international agenda, and fully implement the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

He also called for improving governance rules in emerging fields, turning new frontiers such as the deep sea, the polar regions and outer space into areas for international cooperation, and evolving an AI governance structure based on general consensus soon.

Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, the forum is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World."

Nearly 400 representatives from strategic, political, academic, business, media, and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN, attended the opening ceremony.(RSS)

title: Historic FRLD decision opens climate finance support for Nepal - The Rising Nepal
description: Historic FRLD decision opens climate finance support for Nepal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct. 25: For the first time in its history, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has decided to provide US$20 million (around Rs. 3 billion) in grant assistance to Nepal to support rehabilitation and reconstruction following the devastating floods of August 26, 2026, which claimed 1,500 lives, left more than 5,000 people missing and affected over 60,000 others.

At its special meeting on October 22, the FRLD board decided to provide Nepal the grant assistance under the Barbados Implementation Modality (BIM) framework.

The decision followed a formal request for assistance submitted to the FRLD on August 31, 2026, by Minister of Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary and Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle. The request came after devastating floods affected 15,000 households, primarily in three districts — Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

To access the grant assistance, Nepal will have to submit a project proposal and implement urgent climate actions on the ground.

The FRLD was established in 2023 to help countries deal with climate-related losses and damage. The decision is historic because the FRLD has not previously decided to allocate money to any country, making Nepal the first to receive such an allocation, said Manjeet Dhakal, Lead Advisor to the Chair of the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group on Climate Change.

“The Fund is intended to support the reconstruction and rehabilitation of areas affected by the Bhotekoshi flood. However, the money has only been allocated at this stage. Nepal must complete the necessary procedures and submit a proposal to access the funds,” Dhakal said.

Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, spokesperson and chief of the Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Forests and Environment, said Nepal had requested assistance from the FRLD to address climate-related losses and damage caused by the devastating Bhotekoshi disaster. The Fund responded by giving the request a high priority and holding a special board meeting to discuss Nepal’s situation.

“Bringing representatives together to discuss Nepal’s request at a special meeting demonstrates the importance the Fund has attached to our situation. We should recognise and appreciate this response. At the same time, we must acknowledge that this allocation alone will not be enough. Nepal needs to mobilise additional resources, improve its budgetary systems and undertake the necessary work through its own institutions,” Dr. Maheshwar said.

Further steps to access the funds

“The FRLD will provide us with guidelines on the documents we need to submit and the procedures we must follow. Based on those guidelines, we will prepare and submit a proposal. Once we complete the required process and submit the proposal, it will be presented at the FRLD’s next board meeting for endorsement. After the board approves it, the project can move towards implementation,” Dr. Maheshwar said.

The proposal will reflect the government’s priorities, policies and laws, as well as the findings of the Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment (RDNA). The National Planning Commission will identify priorities based on the losses and damage suffered and the measures needed for recovery. The proposal will then be prepared accordingly.

According to Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, the FRLD’s next board meeting is scheduled for December. Following its recent online board meeting, Nepal expects to receive guidance on the required documents, procedures and timeline before finalising its approach.

Dhakal said Nepal would need to explain how the money would be used in its proposal. As this is the Fund’s first such allocation decision, there is no precedent to indicate how long the process might take. However, the FRLD was established to respond to situations like this and provide financial support to countries facing severe losses and damage. Nepal therefore hopes the process will be relatively straightforward, he said.

The government can submit the proposal directly or work through institutions accredited to other climate funds. These include the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) and other eligible national institutions. International organisations, including United Nations agencies, may also help facilitate the process.

Nepal has evidence of the role of climate change in the disaster. The World Weather Attribution report provides information on the unusually high temperatures in the affected region. Similarly, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)'s rapid disaster needs assessment provides details of the extent of the damage and losses, Dhakal said.

Nepal will submit its proposal within the timeframe specified by the Fund, Dr. Maheshwar said. “If the Fund asks us to submit the proposal within a week, we will do so within a week. If it gives us two weeks or a month, we will work within that timeframe. We are waiting for its guidance.”

Concerns over adequacy of funds

Dr. Maheshwar said the amount allocated by the FRLD would not cover the entire cost of recovery from the Bhotekoshi disaster. “I have never assumed that the entire cost of recovery would come from a single fund, institution or country,” he said.

Nepal must identify and access different sources of finance. Government employees have contributed more than 10 days’ salary to support the affected people. Other sources include the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, the national budget and resources available through the three tiers of government. The private sector and international community are also potential sources of support.

Nepal still needs to discuss grants, loans and other forms of assistance with international partners. It would be unrealistic to expect a single funding allocation to cover the entire cost of recovery.

Dhakal said Nepal should also explore other sources of climate finance, including the Adaptation Fund and the Green Climate Fund.

“We need to mobilise resources from different sources and use them in the country’s best interests. There are several climate funds that Nepal can approach. The Adaptation Fund has also indicated that it will discuss related issues, and Nepal can submit proposals to the Green Climate Fund as well,” he said.

How the money will be channelled

The money is likely to be channelled through an agency, as the Fund has its own procedures and requirements. Nepal is waiting for guidance on whether it must work through an already accredited institution or whether other arrangements will be permitted, Dr. Maheshwar said.

“One possible option is to channel the money through the government’s systems. We are open to receiving the funds through the government’s treasury system if the FRLD permits this arrangement. However, we have not yet assumed that the money will be transferred directly to the national treasury,” he said.

According to Dhakal, the money is not intended for immediate relief, as that phase has already passed. The focus should now be on reconstruction and rehabilitation, including restoring the lives and livelihoods of affected communities. The assistance should be viewed from a broader perspective than climate change adaptation alone.

Nepal’s recovery efforts will also depend on contributions through the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, public fundraising, development partners and other organisations, as well as government allocations through the national budget.

According to Dhakal, the decision could also provide a pathway for other countries facing similar disasters in the future. Although Nepal is the first country to receive such an allocation from the FRLD, the experience may help demonstrate how financial support can be mobilised for countries facing climate-related loss and damage.

title: No polio cases reported, but risk remains - The Rising Nepal
description: No polio cases reported, but risk remains  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter,Kathmandu, Oct. 25: On World Polio Day, various organisations and experts have expressed concern about eradicating the disease and held several programmes.

The World Polio Day is commemorated globally every year on October 24th and is dedicated to raising awareness for the eradication of polio.

Prof. Dr. Shrijana Shrestha, Chairperson of the World Health Organization’s South-East Asia Regional Certification Commission for Polio Eradication, said that while Nepal’s achievements in eradicating polio are remarkable, sustained effort is required to maintain this status indefinitely.

In a video message released on Saturday on the occasion of World Polio Day, Chair Dr. Shrestha added that sustained efforts are essential to maintain Nepal’s polio-free status.

She also emphasized the need for constant vigilance, given the open borders and the movement of people, noting that as long as the polio virus exists anywhere in the world, there remains a risk of the disease entering Nepal.Dr. Shrestha further stressed five key priorities for maintaining Nepal’s polio-free status.

The first is to ensure the delivery of routine immunization services, specifically guaranteeing that every child, especially those in remote or high-risk areas and communities, receives a full course of vaccinations.

In addition, she stated that it is essential to strengthen surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis to ensure the timely detection of the polio virus, and to conduct regular reviews of surveillance data to guarantee a rapid and effective response should the virus be detected.

She added that given the shifting landscape of global financial support for polio, it is crucial to preserve the essential capacities and infrastructure required for the surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases, laboratory services, immunization programmes, and outbreak response.

“Leveraging the experience, expertise, and infrastructure gained through polio eradication efforts to strengthen surveillance and response systems for other vaccine-preventable diseases is needed,” she said.

According to experts, the presence of polio in even a single country means that all nations remain at risk. Polio is caused by a virus that enters the body, affects the intestines, and spreads to the nervous system; it can lead to infections in the mouth and facial area, cause muscle weakness, and result in paralysis.

Experts suggest that to eradicate this disease, there is a strong emphasis on vaccinating children under the age of five. The Nepal Government has been providing free polio vaccinations to children across the country by mobilizing rural female health volunteers.

The government data show that currently there are zero confirmed cases of polio in Nepal. However, to maintain polio-free status, the government, including the WHO, is conducting intensive surveillance across the country. According to data released in 2025, at least 579 suspected polio cases were identified and tested nationwide; however, polio was not confirmed in any of these cases.

Back in 2014, the WHO declared Nepal a polio-free country. The last case of polio in Nepal was detected in 2010 in Rautahat district. Public health experts argue that although there are no polio cases in Nepal, the risk of infection has not yet been eliminated. Since polio has not been completely eradicated in neighboring countries and several other nations worldwide, the threat of the virus entering Nepal remains.

Meanwhile, special polio vaccination campaigns have also been conducted from time to time in the capital, Kathmandu, and border with India to prevent the virus from entering.

title: PHP2Shell security flaw forces thousands of Nepali websites offline - The Kathmandu Post
description: PHP2Shell security flaw forces thousands of Nepali websites offline  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Thousands of government and banking websites in Nepal have been taken offline as a precaution after two critical security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language widely used to build and run websites.

The PHP Foundation, which maintains the language, disclosed the vulnerabilities and released security patches on October 21. Websites began going offline around the world as governments, financial institutions and other organisations moved to protect their systems against potential attacks.

In Nepal, thousands of government websites run on a shared template, allowing authorities to take them offline centrally. As a result, web portals operated by ministries, departments, commissions and other government offices have become inaccessible.

Nepal Rastra Bank’s official website and web-based services have also been temporarily suspended. Private banks and financial institutions have issued notices saying they have shut down their websites and digital services while strengthening security.

The Vehicle Consignment Tracking System (VCTS), operated by the Department of Revenue Investigation to track freight vehicles, is also offline. The department said it had suspended the service because of serious security vulnerabilities in PHP and related technologies, citing the risk of exploitation.

“Vehicles may continue to operate with the relevant documents, including bills and invoices issued in accordance with existing rules. Once the system is back online, the relevant service users, taxpayers and agencies must issue VCTS records as required without delay,” the department said in a notice.

The service will resume after the necessary security updates have been installed, the department said.

The central bank has urged all banks and financial institutions, payment system operators and service providers to step up security monitoring of their systems.

It remains uncertain whether all government websites will be operational when offices reopen on Monday after the week-long Dashain holiday. The Software Development and Operation Centre (SDOC), under the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, expects thousands of government websites to return online together by Monday or Tuesday.

Kiran Timilsina, the centre’s chief executive officer, said systems that do not use PHP had been brought back online from October 22, while the remaining systems were undergoing audits.

Keeping the websites offline during the holiday had helped limit the immediate risks and disruption, he said.

“Most Nepal government websites run on a shared platform called GIWIMS, which is now being audited,” Timilsina said. “The necessary technical decisions will be taken by Sunday evening. Once we patch the platform centrally, thousands of government websites will come back online together, from Sunday evening through Monday or Tuesday.”

The holiday had helped minimise inconvenience to the public because government offices were closed, he said. Work was under way to restore the websites before offices reopened on Monday.

Engineers from the National Cyber Security Centre and the Integrated Data Management Centre are also working with the SDOC to restore the systems safely, the heads of the agencies told Kantipur. They said they had begun taking systems offline as soon as they learned of the PHP problem on the day of Dashain tika.

The National Cyber Security Centre issued an advisory on October 22 and designated its computer officer, Ashish Bhatt, as the focal person to coordinate the response, said Raj Kumar Maharjan, the centre’s director and spokesperson. The centre has instructed organisations to update their systems.

“The systems were shut down as a precaution,” Maharjan said. “There have been no cases of unauthorised access or cyberattacks in Nepal linked to this issue so far.”

The shutdowns have nevertheless disrupted online information and public services.

One challenge is that some systems run on older PHP versions, including version 8.1 and earlier, which have reached the end of their supported life and no longer receive official security updates from the PHP project.

“Because PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported, official security patches or fixes are not available for them,” a government IT engineer said. “Although PHP has suggested some temporary measures for older versions, upgrading to a newer version and installing the patch is a better long-term solution than relying on workarounds. But that takes time.”

The SDOC has said systems will be restored in stages after security patching and testing are complete.

A patch is a software update released by developers to correct errors or close security vulnerabilities in a programme’s code. Such updates are commonly called security patches. Since official patches are not generally available for obsolete PHP versions, systems running them may need to be upgraded to a supported version before they can be secured.

Why is the restoration taking so long?

On the evening of October 21, the PHP Foundation disclosed two security vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together, they are known as PHP2Shell.

Developers typically release patches when disclosing security flaws. But distributing and activating an update across different servers, cloud systems and user environments can take time, Timilsina said. Depending on the systems involved, it can take anything from a few hours to a week for patches to reach all affected infrastructure and be applied.

This delay has slowed the restoration of websites taken offline as a precaution.

“We installed the patch on the centre’s website and some other systems on the night of October 21 and brought them back online,” Timilsina said. “Other systems, such as mail servers that do not use PHP, were restored the following day. The remaining systems are being audited.”

Installing a new security patch alone is not enough to resolve the problem in older systems, he said. The centre had also found that source code for some legacy systems had not been audited.

“We are prioritising source-code audits to identify other potential vulnerabilities that may already exist in these older systems, alongside upgrading them to newer versions,” he said.

For systems covered by annual maintenance contracts, the relevant vendors are responsible for addressing the problem, with the SDOC providing coordination and support. For systems without such contracts, the centre is reviewing source code and handover documentation before deciding how each should be handled.

“Systems belonging to essential agencies, such as the Public Service Commission, need to be brought back online quickly,” Timilsina said. “The holiday has delayed access to documentation and hosting details, but the systems should be back online by Sunday and Tuesday.”

Some banks, including Nabil Bank, Sanima Bank and Nepal Investment Mega Bank, have already updated their systems and resumed services after temporary disruptions.

How did the vulnerability emerge?

International media reports, citing cybersecurity firm Wiz, say PHP powers more than 70 percent of websites worldwide.

According to Wiz, a cybersecurity research firm owned by Google, the global alert was triggered by long-standing flaws in PHP’s core engine.

If exploited, the flaws could allow attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers and steal sensitive data. Security advisories say the vulnerabilities can be exploited remotely without authentication.

In a BBC report, technology reporter Liv McMahon and business reporter Osmond Chia said the flaws had gone undetected for years and were difficult for human researchers to identify. The vulnerabilities came to light with assistance from OpenAI’s artificial intelligence models and researchers from Wiz and Calif.

The discovery triggered a global response. The BBC reported that websites and online services had been taken offline in several countries, including Finland and the Netherlands, as organisations worked to secure their systems. Japan’s telecommunications and IT provider SoftBank Corp also suspended earthquake, tsunami and other emergency alert services until Monday, according to the report.

International cybersecurity agencies, including the US National Security Agency, have advised organisations to isolate systems that cannot be patched immediately from the internet.

The PHP Foundation has released patched versions of the language, including PHP 8.2.35 plus, 8.3.36 plus, 8.4.27 plus and 8.5.12 plus.

Cybersecurity specialists say organisations should first identify which PHP version is running on their servers, then use official scanning tools to determine whether their systems are vulnerable.

Once a vulnerability is confirmed, the system should be upgraded to a secure PHP version. Maharjan said users should download and install patches only from official PHP links or trusted package managers, not from unauthorised or suspicious sources.

Installing a patch is not enough on its own. PHP-FPM, Apache and all other PHP services running in the background must also be restarted to ensure the updated security code takes effect.

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Recent developments in Nepal highlight the country’s progress in climate adaptation, infrastructure recovery, food security and tourism, alongside persistent challenges in disaster management and public infrastructure. The Adaptation Fund’s approval of climate adaptation projects, with proposed funding of USD 44.9 million, offers opportunities to strengthen early warning systems, protect ecosystems and build resilient communities. However, effective implementation and timely access to climate finance will be essential to translate these commitments into tangible benefits.

Meanwhile, the estimated Rs 70 million reconstruction cost for the flood-damaged Beni–Darbang–Muna road underscores the economic and connectivity challenges posed by increasingly disruptive weather events. Restoring this vital route is important for local mobility, trade and access to public services.

Nepal’s planned tourism cooperation with India and the sharp increase in visitors to Mustang indicate opportunities to expand tourism markets and support local businesses. Nevertheless, seasonal road disruptions, traffic congestion and high-altitude mountaineering risks highlight the need for safer transport infrastructure, effective visitor management and stronger emergency response systems. The recovery of two Japanese climbers’ bodies from Mount Gangapurna also underscores the dangers associated with high-altitude expeditions.

In food security, Nepal’s improved Global Hunger Index score and declining child stunting rate indicate progress in nutrition. However, its moderate hunger classification signals that further efforts remain necessary. Overall, sustainable development will depend on coordinated investment in climate resilience, reliable infrastructure, tourism safety and long-term food security.

Adaptation Fund approves three climate adaptation projects for Nepal

The Adaptation Fund has approved three climate adaptation project proposals for Nepal aimed at strengthening vulnerable communities, protecting ecosystems through nature-based solutions and improving early warning systems for floods and landslides. The proposals were approved at the Fund’s 47th Board Meeting, which was also attended by Nepal’s representative on the Adaptation Fund Board, Naresh Sharma. Sharma said the projects would help communities exposed to climate change build resilience, conserve ecosystems and improve preparedness for climate-related disasters through stronger early warning systems. One of the approved proposals is the Green Koshi project, to be implemented by the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC). According to Sharma, the Board approved the project’s concept note with a proposed budget of USD 9.92 million. The initiative aims to strengthen climate resilience and conserve ecosystems through nature-based solutions.

Reconstruction of Beni–Darbang–Muna road estimated to cost Rs 70 million

The reconstruction of the flood- and landslide-damaged Beni–Darbang–Muna road in Myagdi is estimated to cost around Rs 70 million. The road, which connects Mangala, Malika and Dhaulagiri rural municipalities in western Myagdi with the district headquarters, Beni, suffered extensive damage from floods, landslides and erosion along the Myagdi River following continuous rainfall from September 23 to 27. According to the Infrastructure Development Office in Myagdi, around 22 locations along the road from Beni to Muna, the administrative centre of Dhaulagiri Rural Municipality, have been damaged. Engineer Mohan Ruwali of the office said the disasters had washed away road surfaces and severely damaged gabion walls, retaining walls and paved sections.

Nepal–India tourism networking event scheduled for October 26–28

The Nepal–India Cross Border Tourism Connect 2026 will be held from October 26 to 28 through a joint initiative of the Non-Resident Nepali Association International Coordination Council and the Samriddha Chitwan Campaign. The event aims to strengthen tourism cooperation between Nepal and India, link Nepali destinations with international markets and establish direct business connections between tourism operators in both countries. Twenty-one tourism representatives from major Indian cities are expected to participate in business meetings, familiarisation tours and tourism package development. The initiative also seeks to develop an integrated regional tourism circuit connecting Lumbini, Ramgram, Devghat, Nawalpur and Chitwan, covering several local municipalities.

Minister Chaudhary announces approval of three climate projects worth $44.9 million

Minister for Agriculture, Forestry and Environment Gita Chaudhary has highlighted the approval of three climate adaptation projects for Nepal by the Adaptation Fund at its 47th Board Meeting. The projects have a combined proposed value of USD 44.9 million and are intended to strengthen climate resilience and reduce disaster risks. The allocations include USD 9.9 million for the Green Koshi project, implemented by the National Trust for Nature Conservation; USD 30 million for regional flood and landslide early warning systems through the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD); and USD 4.9 million for community resilience initiatives in Lumbini Province through the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat). Chaudhary described the approvals as an important achievement that could help Nepal address the growing economic burden of climate change and strengthen disaster preparedness.

Nepal ranks 72nd in Global Hunger Index 2026, showing improvement

Nepal has ranked 72nd among 122 countries in the Global Hunger Index 2026, scoring 14.5 points and falling into the moderate hunger category. The score marks an improvement from 18.4 in 2018, indicating progress in reducing hunger. In South Asia, Sri Lanka ranks 53rd with 10.2 points, ahead of Nepal, while Bangladesh stands at 84th, India at 100th, Pakistan at 106th and Afghanistan at 108th. The regional average score of 23.5 remains above the global average of 18.1. Nepal’s child stunting rate among children under five declined from 55.9 percent in 2000 to 26.2 percent in 2026. Despite this progress, further efforts are needed to improve nutrition and food security. The index evaluates hunger through four indicators: inadequate calorie intake, child stunting, child wasting and under-five mortality. Lower scores indicate better outcomes.

More than 7,800 tourists visit Mustang in two days after Dashain Tika

Tourist arrivals in Mustang have increased sharply following the Dashain festival and the reopening of the Beni–Jomsom highway, which had been obstructed by monsoon-related landslides on September 27. According to police records, 5,663 tourists visited the district between Ghatasthapana and Vijaya Dashami, including 3,738 men and 1,925 women. Foreign nationals accounted for 4,409 visitors, or 77.85 percent of the total. Arrivals rose further in the two days following Dashain Tika, when 7,846 domestic and international tourists entered Mustang. Of these, 3,033 arrived on Thursday and 4,813 on Friday. Previous monthly figures recorded 30,534 visitors from mid-July to mid-August, at least 20,268 from mid-August to mid-September, and 18,601 from mid-September to mid-October. Local tourism businesses expect visitor numbers to continue rising at major destinations, including Muktinath Temple and Lo Manthang.

Heavy traffic congestion reported at Kathmandu Valley entry points

Major entry points into the Kathmandu Valley are experiencing heavy traffic as people return to the capital following the annual festive holidays. Traffic monitoring reports indicate long queues along key routes, including Nagdhunga–Kalanki, Jadibuti–Koteshwor, Jagati and Dakshinkali–Farping. Official transport records show that more than 576,000 passengers left the capital between Ghatasthapana and October 20 to celebrate the festivals with their families in their home districts. With holidaymakers returning, traffic police have increased monitoring and deployed personnel to manage congestion at major checkpoints. Under normal conditions, approximately 1,000 vehicles pass through the main checkpoints each day, but the continuing return of travellers is putting additional pressure on major roads and entry corridors.

Bodies of two missing Japanese climbers recovered from Mount Gangapurna

Rescue teams have recovered the bodies of two Japanese mountaineers from the southern slopes of Mount Gangapurna at an altitude of approximately 6,300 metres. The climbers went missing while attempting to ascend the 7,455-metre peak in Nyeshyang Rural Municipality-6. Helicopters and high-altitude rescue teams were mobilised after contact with the climbers was lost above 7,050 metres on October 15. Search teams initially found climbing equipment and backpacks along the route towards the summit. Local officials said preparations were underway to transport the bodies to Kathmandu for post-mortem examinations. Authorities will then coordinate with the Japanese Embassy in Kathmandu to facilitate the handover of the remains to the climbers’ families.

title: Curbing Social Media-related Crimes - The Rising Nepal
description: Curbing Social Media-related Crimes  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Social media (SoMe), a byproduct of the information and communication technology (ICT) revolution, has impacted human life beyond imagination. It has encroached upon the privacy of individuals and is an entrenched, pervasive tool capable of overturning a regime. SoMe has its own pros and cons. It has also divided people into two classes: the creators and the receivers or users of those SoMe platforms. Those having technical know-how and resources have become the creators, and those lacking both prerequisites have turned into users. The developed countries have reaped the benefits from SoMe, while the poor countries like Nepal have benefited less from and lost more to SoMe platforms.

The brighter part is that SoMe has connected people from around the world, including those living in remote villages in Nepal. But the darker side is that opportunities come with social and financial costs. The social consequences are long-lasting and perilous. The much-hyped boon of connectivity has an equally disturbing reality. It has connected people living poles apart and estranged people living under one roof. The impact is intangible, but the cost is irrecoverable.

Alarming part

In Nepal's context, where people have merely become consumers of SoMe platforms, disadvantages outweigh advantages. SoMe-related crimes are rising, which were unheard of just a decade ago. The most alarming part is that the state and non-state actors’ efforts to contain SoMe-related crimes have not been so effective. Based on the recent data available, a five-year timeline covering 2021 to 2025 has been taken as a reporting period. According to Facts of Nepal, which mines data from government agencies, the popular SoMe platform Facebook/Messenger tops the list of crimes committed by abusing it. The Facebook/Messenger-related crimes rose from 2021 to 2023 with 4,114 cases registered in 2021, and 5,492 in 2022, culminating in a staggering number of cases of 14,603 in 2023.

TikTok is the second biggest contributor to SoMe-related crimes. The number of offenses that occurred via the video-sharing site stands at 131; 501; 1,027; 1,598 and 6,069 over the five years, respectively. The third is WhatsApp. A total of 69; 205; 826; 1,968 and 2,720 crimes were committed using this site in the reporting years in sequence, which has gone up sharply in recent years. Other SoMe platforms misused to commit crimes, from petty ones to big financial scams, include Viber, Imo, YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, website hacking, email, online payment systems (eSewa as recorded in the report), and others. The total number of crimes related to those platforms was 4,751; 6,948; 18,138 and 19,563 in the five-year reporting period, respectively.

There has been a phenomenal growth in the use of mobile phones in Nepal over a decade. According to the Economic Survey 2025/26, by mid-March 2026, there are over 30 million telephone users in Nepal, including cellular mobile phone users. Nepal Telecom Authority (NTA) data shows that the number of people using data/internet provided by NEA-licensed internet service providers is north of 40 million by mid-March 2026. The rising use of mobile phones, coupled with wider internet coverage, has given rise to the use and misuse of SoMe.

Increased access to SoMe has fueled online financial scams. Facts of Nepal reports that financial scams committed using online payment systems have grown steadily over the past five years. Crimes related to payments committed through eSewa, an online payment platform, alone were 50 in 2021; 137 in 2022; 348 in 2023; 430 in 2024; and 745 in 2025. SoMe has been misused to take revenge, harass, and bully people. The perpetrators are mostly male, and the victims are mostly female, followed by gender and sexual minorities. It appears that there is a contradictory but corresponding relationship between the rising SoMe-related crimes. On the one hand, people have become aware of a legal provision that penalises wrongdoers and have increasingly been reporting such cases to the police.

Consequences

On the other hand, those SoMe misusers who commit crimes seem unaware of the consequences of their misconduct. A few years ago, a boy from Nuwakot district posted a message on his Facebook wall about the availability of turtle hatchlings. He didn’t know that it was illegal to keep turtles. So, the two sides - low level of digital literacy and growing level of awareness of reporting scams - coexist. The ease of creating fake accounts also prompts idiots to harass or cheat people, taking advantage of loopholes in technology. And perhaps we lack the technology and expertise to trace such perpetrators. This is why the crimes related to SoMe have been rising continuously.

Another contributing factor is extremely low institutional capacity. The Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police, the only law-enforcing agency, remains quite neglected by the state in terms of strengthening its institutional capacity. According to available data, by August 2024, there are 106 personnel in the central Cyber Bureau, with just 28 assigned to the IT department. The government should recruit more personnel, equip them, and train them in new technologies to prevent crimes. Merge the Armed Police Force with Nepal Police to strengthen its capacity. How can 28 officials investigate cybercrimes that have been rising steadily? The wrongdoers are always one step ahead of the police. How can the government formed on the promise of improving governance afford to ignore the capacity of the authority entrusted with public safety?

title: Fixtures unveiled for Nepal's historic T20 World Cup co-hosting - The Rising Nepal
description: Fixtures unveiled for Nepal's historic T20 World Cup co-hosting  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
BY A STAFF REPORTER, Kathmandu, Oct. 25: Nepal will host the ICC U19 Women’s T20 World Cup for the first time alongside Bangladesh from January 21 to February 6, 2027, with the International Cricket Council (ICC) unveiling the groups and fixtures for the tournament.

The Tribhuvan University (TU) International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur and Mulpani Cricket Ground in Kathmandu will host matches in Nepal, while Chattogram and Sylhet will stage games in Bangladesh.

Nepal have been drawn in Group A alongside India, Ireland and the West Indies, with all their group-stage matches scheduled at the TU Cricket Ground in Kirtipur.

Nepal will begin their campaign against Ireland on January 22 before facing India on January 24. They will conclude their group-stage fixtures against the West Indies on January 26.

The tournament will feature four groups, with the top three teams from each group advancing to the Super Six stage, which begins on January 27. The semi-finals and final will be held in Chattogram, Bangladesh.

The tournament marks a significant milestone for Nepalese cricket, providing the country with an opportunity to showcase its infrastructure and organisational capabilities while giving the home side a chance to compete against some of the leading teams in women’s youth cricket.

Ahead of the global event, the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) has scheduled two preparatory tours in November to strengthen the team’s match fitness and tactical readiness.

Nepal’s preparation will begin with the Belt and Road series in China from November 3 to 8. The team will play six matches against Thailand, China and Hong Kong, China, facing each opponent twice.

Nepal will open the series against Thailand on November 3 before taking on China on November 4 and Hong Kong, China, on November 5. The return fixtures will see Nepal face Thailand again on November 6, China on November 7 and Hong Kong, China, on November 8.

Following the China tour, Nepal will travel to Bengaluru, India, for a tri-series at the Centre of Excellence (COE) from November 12 to 22. The competition will feature India A and India B alongside Nepal, offering the young players an opportunity to test themselves against strong opposition.

Nepal are scheduled to face India B on November 12 and India A on November 14.

They will meet India A again on November 20, before the final is scheduled for November 22.

The two preparatory assignments are expected to provide Nepal with valuable international exposure ahead of their home World Cup campaign. Matches against regional opponents in China will help the squad build consistency, while the Bengaluru series will offer a more demanding test against India’s youth teams.

Playing a World Cup on home soil will bring added expectations for Nepal’s young cricketers. Their performances in the November tours will be important in assessing the team’s readiness, identifying areas for improvement and building combinations ahead of the tournament.

With the World Cup approaching, Nepal will look to make the most of their preparation schedule and home advantage as they prepare to compete against established cricketing nations on the global stage.
